title: Route 66 Turns 100: A Road Trip Through a Century of Pop Culture
summary:
America's most famous highway just turned 100. Route 66 was created in 1926, and it still draws travelers who want to drive from Chicago to Santa Monica, California — more than 2,000 miles through eight states, past big cities, small towns, and deserts.

The road earned its nickname, 'the Mother Road,' from writer John Steinbeck. His 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath followed families traveling Route 66 west during the Dust Bowl, a time in the 1930s when drought and dust storms forced many families to leave their farms and look for work in California. The book won a Pulitzer Prize and became a film.

Route 66 has its own soundtrack, too. Songwriter Bobby Troup wrote the famous tune '(Get Your Kicks on) Route 66' in 1946 during a road trip to California. Nat King Cole made it a hit, and singers and bands from Bing Crosby to Chuck Berry, the Rolling Stones, and Depeche Mode have recorded their own versions.

After World War II, family road trips took off, and Route 66 became a screen star. A TV show named Route 66 followed two young friends driving across America in a Corvette. The 1969 film Easy Rider sent three travelers down the highway by motorcycle. In 2006, Pixar's animated movie Cars set its story in Radiator Springs, a made-up town on Route 66, and it inspired a theme-park ride at Disneyland's California Adventure.

The highway was officially retired as a federal road in 1985, but its magic never faded. Today, travelers still stop at retro diners, roadside motels, and quirky roadside attractions. Route 66 expert Michael Wallis, whose 1990 book The Mother Road helped bring the road back, says the road is all about adventure — and a peek at a dream.
why_it_matters: Route 66 shows how a road can shape a country's stories, songs, and movies, and why places tied to shared memories can stay meaningful long after they stop serving their original purpose.

background_read: Route 66 is a famous American highway that runs from Chicago in the east to Santa Monica, California in the west, passing through big cities, small towns, and deserts.
It was built to link the Midwest with the West Coast, giving travelers and families moving west a single road to follow.
Over time it became much more than a road: writers, musicians, and filmmakers turned it into a symbol of freedom, adventure, and the classic American road trip.
Even though it is no longer an official federal highway, people still drive it today to see its retro diners, roadside motels, and quirky attractions.
